verses.text: Now on the third day, Esther put on her royal clothing, and stood in the inner court of the king’s house, next to the king’s house. The king sat on his royal throne in the royal house, next to the entrance of the house.

When the king saw Esther the queen standing in the court, she obtained favor in his sight; and the king held out to Esther the golden scepter that was in his hand. So Esther came near, and touched the top of the scepter.
Then the king asked her, “What would you like, queen Esther? What is your request? It shall be given you even to the half of the kingdom.”
Esther said, “If it seems good to the king, let the king and Haman come today to the banquet that I have prepared for him.”
Then the king said, “Bring Haman quickly, so that it may be done as Esther has said.” So the king and Haman came to the banquet that Esther had prepared.
The king said to Esther at the banquet of wine, “What is your petition? It shall be granted you. What is your request? Even to the half of the kingdom it shall be performed.”
Then Esther answered and said, “My petition and my request is this.

If I have found favor in the sight of the king, and if it please the king to grant my petition and to perform my request, let the king and Haman come to the banquet that I will prepare for them, and I will do tomorrow as the king has said.”
Then Haman went out that day joyful and glad of heart, but when Haman saw Mordecai in the king’s gate, that he didn’t stand up nor move for him, he was filled with wrath against Mordecai.
Nevertheless Haman restrained himself, and went home. There, he sent and called for his friends and Zeresh his wife.

Haman recounted to them the glory of his riches, the multitude of his children, all the things in which the king had promoted him, and how he had advanced him above the princes and servants of the king.
Haman also said, “Yes, Esther the queen let no man come in with the king to the banquet that she had prepared but myself; and tomorrow I am also invited by her together with the king.
Yet all this avails me nothing, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king’s gate.”

Then Zeresh his wife and all his friends said to him, “Let a gallows be made fifty cubits  high, and in the morning speak to the king about hanging Mordecai on it. Then go in merrily with the king to the banquet.” This pleased Haman, so he had the gallows made.

footnotes.content: Three days of prayer. Then robes, courage, and the terrible risk of stepping uninvited before the king. Esther knew the law as well as anyone—she could die for this. But there are moments when we stop measuring our safety and start trusting the God who has hidden us for a purpose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The scepter extended—that gesture turns everything. What was forbidden becomes mercy in a single moment. The king's favor is her life, but deeper still: grace acts without our earning. She touches the scepter, and the invisible hand that has guided her all along becomes visible.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Even to the half of the kingdom." The king speaks extravagantly, as kings do—but Esther holds her silence. Sometimes the hardest courage is knowing what NOT to say, waiting for the right moment. She has already prayed; now she practices the ancient art of patience.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She asks only for a banquet—dinner with the king and Haman. To Ahasuerus, it sounds like a simple pleasure; to Esther, it is a careful web of opportunity. I notice she invites her enemy to the table. Sometimes love and wisdom wear a disguise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king moves with eagerness—Esther's favor has warmed him. Haman is summoned, unaware he is walking toward the scaffold he will soon construct. The hand that holds all things brings both the woman and her enemy to the same table, and only one knows why.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Over wine, the king offers again—even half his kingdom. He is intoxicated not just with drink but with her presence. And still she says nothing of her need. There is a providence in silence; she waits for the moment when speaking will land like a arrow, not like an echo.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "My petition and my request is this." She begins—but does not finish. The incomplete sentence hangs in the air. Her first invitation was the test; her second will be the truth. Even at the height of the king's willingness, she chooses to wait one more night.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She asks for one more dinner—tomorrow, not tonight. Why delay when the king's ear is open? Perhaps she knows that the right moment is not yet ripe, or that Mordecai still lacks something he must understand first. The Lord's timing often means "not yet," even when we have the king's hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Haman leaves the banquet glowing with pride—until he sees Mordecai, who will not bow. One man's dignity breaks Haman's joy into pieces. I have watched pride crumble like this: one small refusal to flatter, and the whole tower of vanity shakes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Home behind closed doors, Haman summons his friends and wife. He will tell them everything—his riches, his children, his rise—as if these words might heal the wound that Mordecai struck. But some wounds cannot be healed by counting our possessions.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He recounts his glory: wealth, children, promotion. These are the metrics by which he measures himself. Yet in this very boasting, he reveals the emptiness underneath—for a man at peace does not need to rehearse his importance. Pride whispers that we are not yet great enough.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Esther let no man come with the king but myself." Haman is still drunk on this small honor. He does not see that Esther is using him, or that the Lord is using Esther. He sees only himself, reflected infinitely in the mirror of his own vanity.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Yet all this avails me nothing." One man, one refusal, one bowed knee withheld—and everything crumbles. Mordecai sits at the gate unbending, and Haman cannot rest. I have seen this: when we build ourselves on the approval of others, a single "no" can undo a thousand "yeses."
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this counsel: how quickly the proud turn to violence when dignity is denied. Zeresh and his friends leap to build the gallows. Looking back from our own time, we see that Haman's hands were making not just a tool of death, but the very means of his own undoing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
